summary: Proposes raising the permitted initial window of TCP from one segment to roughly four kilobytes. A larger start helps short transfers finish faster. It is an experimental specification and was replaced by RFC 3390.

eli5.summary: When TCP starts, it carefully sends just one small package. This idea lets it send a few packages right away, so small downloads finish sooner.

questions: how does tcp initial window affect performance
subtitle: Speeding up short TCP transfers by allowing the first packets to be sent faster.

tldr.problem: TCP traditionally starts with a small congestion window (one segment) to avoid overloading the network. For short transfers like web pages and email that fit in a few kilobytes, this conservative approach is slower than necessary, requiring multiple round-trip times (RTTs) before all data is sent.
tldr.mechanism: Allow TCP to begin with an initial window of up to 4 kilobytes (approximately 2 to 4 segments, depending on segment size) instead of one segment. The exact formula depends on the maximum segment size (MSS): between 2*MSS and 4*MSS, with an upper bound around 4380 bytes.
tldr.outcome: Short transfers finish in fewer RTTs with no significant increase in congestion or packet loss in typical network conditions. RFC 2414 is experimental and has been superseded by RFC 3390, which incorporated this and related changes into the standard TCP congestion control algorithms.

today: RFC 2414 is experimental and was superseded by RFC 3390, which incorporated this and related changes into the standard TCP congestion control specification. The larger initial window mechanism is now widely deployed and is part of standard TCP implementations.

sections.title: The Problem and the Change
sections.content:
TCP uses slow start when opening a new connection to probe the network's available capacity without causing congestion. Traditionally, slow start begins with a congestion window (cwnd) of one segment—typically 512 bytes or 1460 bytes depending on network conditions. The window grows exponentially during slow start: each time the sender receives an acknowledgment, it increases the window by one segment.

For short transfers, particularly HTTP requests and SMTP messages that fit in 4 kilobytes or less, the initial window of one segment causes unnecessary delays. The sender must wait an entire round-trip time (RTT) just to send the second segment, then another RTT for the third, and so on. This can add 200 milliseconds or more to small transfers in the common case where the receiver uses delayed acknowledgments (waiting for two segments to arrive before sending an ACK).

RFC 2414 proposes increasing the permitted initial window to between 2 and 4 segments, subject to an upper limit of roughly 4380 bytes. The precise upper bound is: min(4*MSS, max(2*MSS, 4380 bytes)).
sections.eli5: Right now TCP is timid: it sends one piece, waits, sends the next piece. This RFC says TCP can be braver at the start and send three or four pieces right away. It helps short conversations finish much faster.

sections.title: Benefits of Larger Initial Windows
sections.content:
The RFC identifies three main advantages. First, a receiver using delayed ACKs will send an ACK after the second data segment arrives, eliminating the wait for an ACK timeout (often up to 200 milliseconds with the one-segment window). Second, for short transfers under 4 kilobytes, a larger initial window can reduce total transfer time to a single RTT, significantly improving perceived performance for web browsing and email downloads. Third, for long-duration connections that will eventually reach large congestion windows, the larger initial window eliminates up to three RTTs and a delayed ACK timeout during the slow-start phase, particularly benefiting high-bandwidth, long-propagation-delay connections like those over satellite links.

The RFC also notes that TCP already generates bursts in normal operation: delayed ACKs cause the sender to transmit two or three segments at once during congestion avoidance, and slow start can generate three- to five-segment bursts. A four-segment initial window is not a dramatic departure from existing burst patterns.
sections.eli5: Larger windows help web pages load faster, emails arrive quicker, and satellite links work much better. And TCP already does burst-like behavior, so this is not shocking.

sections.title: Risks and Trade-offs
sections.content:
A larger initial window poses two potential disadvantages: effects on individual connections and effects on the network as a whole. For individual connections, a burst of four segments can sometimes trigger packet drops in heavily congested networks with simple queue management (Drop Tail). If those segments are dropped, the connection may experience an unnecessary retransmit timeout. However, in uncongested networks or networks with active queue management (such as Random Early Detection), premature drops are unlikely.

For the network, the RFC examines three concerns: duplicate segments, segments dropped later in the path, and increased overall packet drop rates. Analysis in the document shows that if one segment from a four-segment initial window is dropped, the sender will not retransmit duplicate segments when using Fast Retransmit recovery. If multiple segments are dropped, the worst case without SACK is transmitting one duplicate segment. The RFC concludes there is no significant danger of congestion collapse from larger initial windows, particularly given the deployment of higher-speed links and improved queue management mechanisms.
sections.eli5: In very crowded networks, the bigger burst might cause some packets to be dropped, and the sender would have to resend them. But in normal networks, it is fine. And you can always dial it back if needed.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations must carefully coordinate the larger initial window with Path MTU Discovery. If the MSS is found to be too large, the congestion window should be reduced by the ratio of the old segment size to the new segment size to prevent large bursts of smaller segments.

The RFC discusses two strategies for handling the "Don't Fragment" (DF) bit when Path MTU Discovery is in use. Setting DF in all initial-window segments will cause all of them to be dropped if the path MTU is too small, triggering a retransmit timeout. Setting DF only on the last segment in the initial window minimizes the chance of unnecessary Fast Retransmit. The RFC leaves this as an open question requiring implementation experience.

The RFC also warns that web browsers should not use larger initial windows as an excuse to open multiple simultaneous TCP connections, as this increases unfairness to other traffic on the network, regardless of the window size.
sections.eli5: When changing the window size, be careful about how big each piece is. And do not let browsers open many connections at once just because the first one is faster.

sections.title: Simulation and Experimental Evidence
sections.content:
The RFC surveys multiple experimental studies of larger initial windows. Over satellite channels with a 512-byte MSS, a four-segment initial window showed throughput improvements of up to 30% depending on transfer size. Over 28.8 kbps dialup modem links, a four-segment window decreased 16 KB file transfer time by roughly 10% with no increase in drop rate. Simulations on hybrid fiber coax (HFC) systems showed reduced page-load times for HTTP transfers.

Network-wide studies are more mixed. For 16 KB transfers to 100 Internet hosts, the drop rate increased slightly (0.04 segments/transfer) while transfer time improved by roughly 25%. Simulations with HTTP and FTP flows sharing a congested gateway showed the larger window generally increased throughput and network power, with drop rate increases typically under 1%, except in one heavily congested scenario where drop rates went from 3.5% to 4.5%. In very congested networks where the bottleneck link can only support one segment per connection, larger initial windows increased both loss rates (by 1-2%) and retransmit timeouts.
sections.eli5: Tests show the bigger window helps short downloads a lot, especially over slow and far-away links. Network-wide tests show it usually helps overall, though very crowded networks might see a tiny bit more packet loss.
